query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Performing a single-step cryogenic rolling followed by a short low-temperature annealing treatment on the eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine the lamellar colony microstructure, reduce the spacing of internal boundaries, and promote the formation of a dual-scale grain/subgrain network that acts as dislocation sinks, thereby overcoming dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations. This should substantially increase the room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even increasing the alloy's strength relative to the untreated material.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure comprised of dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: A single-step cryogenic rolling (cryo-deformation) immediately followed by a short duration annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under standard strain rate conditions; the intervention is applied uniformly to bulk samples.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined hierarchical microstructure featuring uniformly reduced lamellar colony thickness and a dual network of fine grain and subgrain boundaries that dissipate local stresses.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling introduces high dislocation densities while limiting recovery, and the subsequent low-temperature annealing rebalances residual stresses and triggers partial recrystallization where needed. This process tailors the internal boundaries so they serve as efficient dislocation sinks rather than sites for pile-up, thereby reducing local stress concentrations and arresting microcrack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy with significantly higher tensile ductility (improved elongation to failure) while maintaining or slightly increasing yield strength and ultimate tensile strength compared to the untreated state.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dislocation pile-up-induced brittleness and limited ductility under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies under room-temperature conditions and standard tensile testing regimes; the results may vary with changes in strain rate or environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the precise optimization of rolling reduction and annealing parameters necessary to achieve a uniformly refined microstructure across all lamellar colonies. Additionally, the trade-off between strength and ductility may depend subtly on the alloy's exact composition and initial microstructural inhomogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy. Subject half of the samples to the cryogenic rolling followed by low-temperature annealing treatment, while keeping the other half as untreated controls. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests under identical conditions for both groups. Analyze the microstructures using SEM and XRD to assess the change in lamellar colony spacing and grain refinement.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., elongation to failure) while maintaining or increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the control group, or if microstructural analysis fails to show the predicted refinement of lamellar colonies with reduced dislocation pile-up, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.
